No lasers involved. Nor a camera up the "hoo-hah."

You can see the process of a robotic hysterectomy here.

Camera goes in through a hole in the abdomen and the uterus is removed through the vaginal cuff that results when the uterus is separated from the body. This eliminates the need for morcellation, which is a process (not a drill) where whatever organ is chopped up into pieces for removal through small laparoscopic incisions. But since taking out a uterus necessarily leaves a much bigger and convenient hole to go through...we just slide it out of the vagina instead of morcellating it.

There is a "hoo-hah" approach called the Vaginal Hysterectomy, which you can see here. But that is rarely done (at my institution, at least) and no cameras are used.

No lasers involved with either tactic.

Yes, one of the risks of any hysterectomy is damage to the ureters (tubes that bring urine from kidney to bladder) or bowel. Either injury is extremely rare, but they are two of the three most dramatic complications of any pelvic procedure (the third is injury to the internal iliac). Both are repairable but require either General Surgery (bowel injury) or Urogynecology (an OB/GYN subspecialty, ureter injury) on call to fix it immediately.

If you are truly worried then have your surgery done at a big hospital with both Gen Surg and Urogyn on staff.

So this is completely conjecture so take my response with a grain of salt. But I recently listened to an episode of Radiolab regarding black boxes, and in it they discussed anesthesia (getting knocked out). And one of the questions raised was why do some patients wake up mid surgery and why do others not? Anyway, the hypothesis was that to have consciousness, all parts of your brain would have to be able to communicate with each other.

From experiments, it was determined that whilst knocked out, the brain still gives off signals (blips if you will) but the different parts of the brain would blip at different times, so in a sense there was talking but no conversation between the different parts. Ping but no Pong. My guess is that dementia works in a similar fashion where sometimes the signals in the brain connect and sometimes they don't. And that the moments they do connect, creates moments of lucidity.

Anyway, that's my hypothesis. Any person more versed in neuroscience, feel free to correct me.

I do not know and I had to ask my roommate who is a hospice care nurse for dementia and Alzheimer's patients. The answer is we really do not know. There are guesses, but it is more anecdotal than scientific scrutiny.

He says that the brain does not encode in a linear or systematic method. For example, you do not remember youngest then oldest. The brain remembers different pathways in different ways. When dementia or Alzheimer's occurs (I could explain the disease if you wanted me to) it results in some parts of the brain being damaged. If your ability to recall faces is damaged you might still be able to recall names. The most common of this is the ability to play music, a lot of people with extreme Alzheimer's can still play music, e.g. Glen Campbell. Also, different parts of the brain can still function even on the same task. A person might flail violently until they get the spoon in their hands at which point they will eat normally. Why this occurs is really unknown, but the brain constantly sends signals and information. Sometimes these messages going through completely undamaged and lucid thoughts or actions occur.
